newsitem.title: FRANCE: Defeated French Gaullists to anoint Seguin leader.
newsitem.headline: Defeated French Gaullists to anoint Seguin leader.

text.p: France's Gaullist RPR party will anoint left-leaning nationalist Philippe Seguin, a potential rival to President Jacques Chirac, as its leader on Sunday, five weeks after being swept from government in an election upset.

Seguin's election by the conservative party's congress is part of a recomposition of the defeated right, over which the weakened president, forced to yield much of his power to a left-wing government, has had only limited influence.

Seguin, 54, a heavyweight orator who led the "no" campaign in a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht treaty on European union, lost no time in ejecting defeated ex-premier Alain Juppe from the party leadership in a coup mounted against Chirac's wishes.
He has put his rhetorical talent to immediate use in attacking Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin but has not yet come up with a coherent political line for the new opposition.

The former National Assembly speaker has pledged allegiance to Chirac, saying the role of a renovated RPR will be to "relay and support the president's initiatives". The two men have resumed weekly lunch meetings to discuss strategy.
Seguin's supporters and Juppe's have buried the hatchet for the moment and will present a joint motion at Sunday's congress.

But Seguin has irked the head of state by cutting a deal with ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur's faction, and his associates have made clear they see him as a potential candidate to succeed Chirac when the president's term expires in 2002.
"It is not unhelpful that the RPR should contain eminent figures who could aspire to the highest functions of state," former interior minister Charles Pasqua said.

The president has spent much of the last two weeks trying to restore his influence in the party and influence the rebuilding of the right, holding a series of individual meetings with party leaders and defeated members of parliament.

Tension between Chirac and Seguin has centred on the incoming leader's pledge to make Balladur's top lieutenant, former budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, secretary-general of the RPR, the number two slot in the party.
Chirac's inner circle still regards Sarkozy as a traitor who betrayed the legitimate Gaullist leader to run Balladur's 1995 presidential campaign against him.

Balladur has insisted on the appointment of his associate as the price for his support of Seguin, but he acknowleged this week that the question may not be settled on Sunday but left until a national council meeting in the autumn.
Instead, Sarkozy is expected to be given a seat in a collegiate interim leadership.

While the Gaullists have been wrangling over their new leadership, the other main component of the former ruling coalition, the centre-right Union for French Democracy has also promoted two potential presidential rivals.

Free-marketeer Alain Madelin, France's nearest thing to a Thatcherite, was elected leader of the right-wing Republican Party, one of the UDF's two main components, which promptly renamed itself Liberal Democracy.
Former education minister Francois Bayrou, leader of the other main partner, the centrist Democratic Force, was meanwhile elected head of the UDF's parliamentary caucus.
